CORAM:
HON'BLE
MR. JUSTICE GAUTAM KUMAR CHOUDHARY For the Appellant : Mr. Alok Lal, Advocate For Respondent : Mr. Nikhil Ranjan, Advocate For the Appellants : Mr. Nikhil Ranjan,
Advocate For Respondent-Ins. Co. : Mr. Alok Lal, Advocate
Oral Order 17 / Dated : 08.10.2025 I.A. No. 4476 of 2020 in M.A. No. 226 of 2020 1

. Heard learned counsel for the appellants in this interlocutory application which has been filed under Section 5 of the Limitation Act for condonation of delay of 1530 days in filing the instant misc.
appeal.
2.
It is submitted by learned counsel for the appellants that the delay was not intentional and due to financial condition of the appellants, they could not file the appeal within the stipulated time.

3. Motor vehicle Act is a beneficial piece of legislation, and the present applicants are the claimants,
therefore, considering the grounds taken in the interlocutory application, the delay is condoned and the limitation petition is allowed.
4.

The appellant- National Insurance Co. Ltd. is in appeal against the judgment and Award of compensation dated 01.03.2016 passed by learned Principal District Judge-cum-P.O., Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Bokaro, in T.M.V. Claim Case No.18 of 2013 under Section 166 of the M.
V. Act by which the liability to pay the compensation amount has been fixed upon the appellant- Insurance Company.

entities.text: Principal District Judge-cum-P.O., Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Bokaro
entities.label: JUDGE

sentences.text: 5. It is mainly contended on behalf of the insurance company, that liability of the insurance company to indemnify the insured in a Case under section 166 of the MV Act, can arise only if there is some modicum of evidence to show that accident was the result of the rash and negligent driving by the driver of the vehicle under its insurance cover.

Unless there is negligence on the part of the driver which resulted in accident causing death or permanent disability of the third party, the insurance company cannot be held liable to pay compensation 6.
On facts it is argued that there was no fault on the part of the driver of the vehicle which met with accident caused by an unidentified truck.

Preponderance of evidence suggests that the accident resulted not on account of fault of driver of the Indigo car in which the deceased was travelling at the time of accident, but it was a hit and run case.
7.

Accident took place as per the claim application and FIR, on 26.10.2012 at 2:00 pm when the deceased (Minaj Ansari) was going by Indigo Car bearing Registration No.JH-09T-1689 being National Insurance Co. 2 driven by 2025:JHHC:31416 driver-Md. Sayeed Akhtar.

sentences.text: The said vehicle was dashed by an unknown truck, as a result of which, the driver of the car lost control of it and the vehicle dashed into a road-side tree resulting in death of Minaj Ansari.
8. Apart from FIR (Ext.1), reference is made to the deposition of Claimants, CW 1 and CW 2, both of whom have deposed that the accident was the outcome of Indigo Car being dashed by an unknown truck.
9. It was for this reason that the learned Tribunal recorded a finding on issue Nos. II and III that it was not a case of contributory negligence on the part of the driver of the Indigo car.

10. By referring to these facts, it is argued that in absence of any evidence that the driver of the Indigo car was nowhere responsible for the accident and liability has been fastened on the insurer of this car.

11. Reliance is placed on the judgment rendered by Hon'ble the Supreme Court in the case of Surender Kumar Arora and Ors. Vs. Manoj Bisla and Ors., (2012) 4 SCC 552 wherein it was held that it was the responsibility of the claimants to have established that Respondent No.1 was driving the vehicle in a rash and negligent manner which they have failed to do before the Tribunal, as such, the claim under Section 166 of the M. V. Act was not maintainable.

entities.text: Surender Kumar Arora and Ors. Vs. Manoj Bisla and Ors., (2012) 4 SCC 552
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Further, in the case of Oriental Insurance Company Limited vs. Premlata Shukla and Others, reported in (2007) 13 SCC 476 wherein Hon'ble the Supreme Court had occasioned to examine the evidentiary value of the FIR in a claim case, it has been held that rash and negligent driving was sine- qua-non for a claim under Section 166 of the M. V. Act.
12.

entities.text: Oriental Insurance Company Limited vs. Premlata Shukla and Others, reported in (2007) 13 SCC 476
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
It is submitted by learned counsel for the claimants that the witnesses relied upon by learned counsel for the Insurance Company are not the direct eye witness to the accident and, therefore,
their evidence cannot be admitted, so far the manner of accident is concerned.

It is further submitted that the facts of the case are almost similar to that in M.A. No. 48 of 2011 wherein this Court by applying the principle of res ipsa loquitur held the driver of the car to be responsible for causing the accident.
It is argued that there is no evidence to show that the proximate cause of accident was on account of being dashed by a passing truck.
Even if it is assumed that the said truck had been 2025:JHHC:31416 dangerously driven, it could not have resulted in accident without the contributory fault on the part of the driver of the car.
This makes out the case of composite negligence as the deceased was the third party and therefore, the claimant was entitled for compensation from the owner/insurer of the offending car.

In case of composite negligence, a claim application is maintainable against either of the vehicles as held in Khenyei vs. New India Assurance Company Limited and others, 2015 9 SCC 273.
13.

entities.text: Khenyei vs. New India Assurance Company Limited and others, 2015 9 SCC 273
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The main point for determination is, can the owner/ insurer of the insured vehicle be held liable to pay compensation under Section 166 of the M.V. Act, when there is a specific finding on the basis of the evidence on record that there was no fault on the part of the driver of the said vehicle?

3 14.
Legal position so far as Sections 163A and 166 of the M.V. Act is concerned, is not in a shade of doubt.

The former is based on the principle of no-fault liability, whereas the latter is one where the onus is on the claimants to prove that the accident took place due to rash and negligent driving of the vehicle which resulted in the death of the deceased.
Unless and until, the fault on the part of the driver of the offending vehicle is established, a claim under Section 166 of the M.V. Act cannot succeed.

The degree of proof is not like that in a civil or criminal case, as the proceeding before a Motor Vehicle Accident Claim Tribunal is summary in nature and the strict rule of pleading and proof do not apply on it.
Nevertheless, there should be some evidence to draw an inference that the rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle was the proximate cause of accident.
15. FIR is not a substantive piece of evidence however, when it has been adduced into evidence and proved on behalf of the claimant, it cannot be completely brushed aside.

It has been held in National Insurance Company Ltd. Vs. Ratani and others, (2009) 2 SCC 75 ordinarily an allegation made in the F.I.R. would not be substantive evidence per se, but as the F.I.R. is part of the claim application

entities.text: National Insurance Company Ltd. Vs. Ratani and others, (2009) 2 SCC 75
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
,
the same can be looked into.

16. Here in the present case, as per the F.I.R. (Exhibit 1), the accident was caused by rash and negligent driving by a red colour truck which 2025:JHHC:31416 dashed the Indigo car, which lost control of it and dashed against a road side tree.
Consequently, Petarwar P.S. Case No.119/12 was registered under Sections 279, 337, 338, 427, 304A of the I.P.C. against the driver of an unknown truck.
Final Form (Exhibit 2) was also submitted in this case as the unidentified truck could not be traced.
Similar narration of fact is stated to the pleading of the claim application that the accident was on account of rash and negligent driving by the driver of the unknown truck.

17. As rightly argued by the learned counsel on behalf of the Insurance Company, C.W. 1 and C.W. 2,
though not eye witness, but have not attributed the accident to the driver of the Indigo Car, rather have stated in their examination-in-chief on affidavit that the accident was caused by an unknown truck.
It is for this reason that learned Tribunal recorded a finding that it was not a case of contributory negligence.
In the absence of any contrary evidence, there is no reason to differ with the finding of the learned Tribunal on the manner of accident.
The facts of the present case are different from the authority relied upon on behalf of the claimants.
In any case, principle of stare decisis do not apply to disputed questions of fact.

18. In the absence of any pleading or evidence with regard to the negligence on the part of the driver of the offending Indigo car, the claim under Section 166 of the M.V. Act against the owner or the insurer of the vehicle is not sustainable.

The judgment and award of compensation is accordingly,
set aside.

M.A. No.453 of 2016 is allowed and consequently, M.A. No.226 of 2020 stands dismissed.
Pending I.A., if any, stands disposed of.
(Gautam Kumar Choudhary, J.) AKT/Satendra Uploaded 13.10.2025
